items.title: I can describe what an electric field is and explain why it is classified as a vector field
items.what: An electric field is a region of space where a charged particle experiences an electric force. It is a vector field because at every point it has both a magnitude (field strength in N C⁻¹) and a direction, defined as the direction of the force on a small positive test charge placed at that point.
items.why: The vector nature of electric fields means that both magnitude and direction must be specified in any description or diagram. By convention, the direction is defined using a positive test charge, which is a standard that must be applied consistently in all field line diagrams and calculations.
items.example: At a point 0.10 m to the right of a positive charge, the electric field has a magnitude of 1.8 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ and points radially outward (to the right). Both the value and the direction are needed to fully describe the field at that point.

subtopic.name: Electric Field Concepts
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the definition of an electric field as a vector field, the rules for drawing electric field line diagrams around point charges and between parallel plates, and the distinction between electric monopoles and dipoles. It also covers how electric fields compare to gravitational fields.
subtopic.why: The field model is the conceptual foundation for all electric force and energy calculations. Understanding how to draw and interpret field line diagrams is a required practical and exam skill, and distinguishing monopoles from dipoles connects electric fields to both magnetic fields and real-world molecular structures.

items.title: I can draw and interpret electric field line diagrams for a single positive charge and a single negative charge
items.what: For a single positive charge, electric field lines point radially outward in all directions. For a single negative charge, field lines point radially inward toward the charge. In both cases, field lines are more densely packed closer to the charge, indicating a stronger field, and spread out further away.
items.why: Drawing and reading field line diagrams is a core practical and exam skill. The density of lines conveys field strength, and the direction of arrows conveys the force direction on a positive test charge — both are assessed in VCAA examinations.
items.example: A diagram for a +Q charge shows arrows pointing outward like the spokes of a wheel, with the arrows closer to the charge drawn more densely packed. A diagram for a −Q charge has the identical pattern of lines but with all arrows reversed, pointing inward.

subtopic.name: Electric Field Concepts
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the definition of an electric field as a vector field, the rules for drawing electric field line diagrams around point charges and between parallel plates, and the distinction between electric monopoles and dipoles. It also covers how electric fields compare to gravitational fields.

Understanding how to draw and interpret field line diagrams is a required practical and exam skill, and distinguishing monopoles from dipoles connects electric fields to both magnetic fields and real-world molecular structures.

items.title: I can draw and interpret electric field line diagrams for two charges and for parallel plates
items.what: For two opposite charges (a dipole), field lines curve from the positive charge to the negative charge. For two like charges, field lines repel each other and no lines connect the two charges. Between two oppositely charged parallel plates, field lines are straight, parallel, and evenly spaced, representing a uniform field.
items.why: These three configurations appear regularly in VCAA exam questions. The parallel plate case is especially important because it is the basis for all uniform field calculations involving F = qE and W = qV.
items.example: For a +Q and −Q charge placed near each other, field lines leave the positive charge, curve through the space between them, and terminate on the negative charge. Between two oppositely charged parallel plates, the field lines run straight from the positive plate to the negative plate with equal spacing throughout.

items.title: I can state the rules for drawing valid electric field line diagrams
items.what: Electric field lines must run from positive charges to negative charges. They must leave and arrive at conducting surfaces at 90 degrees. Field lines can never cross each other, because crossing would imply the field points in two directions simultaneously at the same point, which is physically impossible.
items.why: Drawing field lines that violate these rules is a common exam error. Understanding why each rule exists (particularly the no-crossing rule) demonstrates deeper conceptual understanding and is rewarded in extended response questions.
items.example: A student draws a field line diagram where two lines cross near a positive charge. This is incorrect: at the crossing point, the field would need to point in two directions at once, which cannot happen. The correct diagram shows lines that curve apart and never intersect.

subtopic.name: Electric Field Concepts
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the definition of an electric field as a vector field, the rules for drawing electric field line diagrams around point charges and between parallel plates, and the distinction between electric monopoles and dipoles. It also covers how electric fields compare to gravitational fields.
subtopic.why: The field model is the conceptual foundation for all electric force and energy calculations. Understanding how to draw and interpret field line diagrams is a required practical and exam skill, and distinguishing monopoles from dipoles connects electric fields to both magnetic fields and real-world molecular structures.

items.title: I can explain the difference between an electric monopole and an electric dipole
items.what: An electric monopole is a single isolated charge — either positive (field lines pointing outward) or negative (field lines pointing inward). An electric dipole consists of two equal and opposite charges separated by a short distance, with field lines running from the positive charge to the negative charge.
items.why: The monopole/dipole distinction is part of the study design glossary and connects to comparisons with gravitational fields (mass is always a gravitational monopole) and magnetic fields (magnetic dipoles have no monopole equivalent). It also has real-world relevance in molecular chemistry.
items.example: A single electron is an electric monopole — its field lines all point inward. A water molecule (H₂O) behaves as an electric dipole because oxygen pulls shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen does, creating a partial negative charge on the oxygen end and partial positive charges on the hydrogen ends.

It also covers how electric fields compare to gravitational fields.
subtopic.why: The field model is the conceptual foundation for all electric force and energy calculations. Understanding how to draw and interpret field line diagrams is a required practical and exam skill, and distinguishing monopoles from dipoles connects electric fields to both magnetic fields and real-world molecular structures.

items.title: I can distinguish between uniform and non-uniform electric fields, and identify electric fields as static or changing
items.what: A uniform electric field has constant strength and direction at all points, represented by evenly spaced parallel field lines. A non-uniform field varies in strength and direction. A static field does not change over time; the fields between charged parallel plates and around stationary point charges are both static.
items.why: These classifications appear directly in the study design and in exam questions. Knowing whether a field is uniform or non-uniform determines which formulas apply, and distinguishing static from changing fields connects this topic to electromagnetic induction studied later.
items.example: The electric field between two parallel charged plates (with fixed charge) is uniform and static — the field lines are parallel and do not change over time. The electric field around a single point charge is non-uniform and static — it is strongest close to the charge and weaker further away, but it does not change unless the charge moves.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the definition of an electric field as a vector field, the rules for drawing electric field line diagrams around point charges and between parallel plates, and the distinction between electric monopoles and dipoles. It also covers how electric fields compare to gravitational fields.

Understanding how to draw and interpret field line diagrams is a required practical and exam skill, and distinguishing monopoles from dipoles connects electric fields to both magnetic fields and real-world molecular structures.

items.title: I can calculate the electric field strength due to a point charge using E = kQ/r²
items.what: The electric field strength at a distance r from a point charge Q is E = kQ/r², where k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². The distance r is measured from the centre of the charge, and the field strength decreases as distance increases following the inverse square law.
items.why: This formula is directly analogous to g = GM/r² for gravitational fields, and understanding the parallel helps consolidate both topics. It is used whenever the field is created by a single isolated charge rather than by parallel plates.
items.example: To find the electric field strength 2.0 m from a charge of +2.0 × 10⁻⁴ C: E = (9.0 × 10⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁴) / (2.0)² = 4.5 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹, directed radially outward from the positive charge.

subtopic.name: Electric Field Calculations
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the two key formulas for electric field strength: E = kQ/r² for a point charge, and E = V/d for a uniform field between parallel plates. It includes the inverse square law behaviour of point charge fields and the calculation of electric force using F = qE.
subtopic.why: These formulas are the quantitative foundation of the entire topic. They appear in almost every VCAA exam question on electric fields, and being able to select and apply the correct formula — point charge versus uniform field — is a critical distinguishing skill at this level.

items.title: I can apply the inverse square law to compare electric field strengths at different distances from a point charge
items.what: Because E ∝ 1/r², doubling the distance from a point charge reduces the field strength to one-quarter, and tripling the distance reduces it to one-ninth. This ratio method can be used even when the charge Q is not given, as long as two distances are known.
items.why: The ratio method is an efficient exam technique for comparing field strengths without recalculating from scratch. It is directly tested in VCAA multiple-choice questions asking students to express the field at one point in terms of the field at another.
items.example: The electric field at point X (10 cm from charge Q) is E₀. Point Y is 20 cm from the same charge — twice the distance. The field at Y is E₀/4, because (10/20)² = 1/4. This can be confirmed: if Q = 8.0 × 10⁻⁸ C, then E at X = 7.2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ and E at Y = 1.8 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ = E₀/4.

subtopic.name: Electric Field Calculations
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the two key formulas for electric field strength: E = kQ/r² for a point charge, and E = V/d for a uniform field between parallel plates. It includes the inverse square law behaviour of point charge fields and the calculation of electric force using F = qE.
subtopic.why: These formulas are the quantitative foundation of the entire topic. They appear in almost every VCAA exam question on electric fields, and being able to select and apply the correct formula — point charge versus uniform field — is a critical distinguishing skill at this level.

items.title: I can calculate the electric field strength between parallel plates using E = V/d
items.what: The electric field strength in the uniform region between two oppositely charged parallel plates is E = V/d, where V is the potential difference between the plates in volts and d is the plate separation in metres. The unit V m⁻¹ is equivalent to N C⁻¹.
items.why: This formula applies whenever a uniform field is produced by parallel plates, and it links electric field strength to voltage — a concept students are familiar with from circuits. The V m⁻¹ unit is commonly used in exam questions and must be recognised as equivalent to N C⁻¹.
items.example: Two parallel plates are separated by 2.0 cm (0.020 m) with a voltage of 100 V across them. The electric field strength is E = 100 / 0.020 = 5000 V m⁻¹. A common error is to use 2.0 instead of 0.020 for the distance, giving an answer 100 times too small.

subtopic.name: Electric Field Calculations
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the two key formulas for electric field strength: E = kQ/r² for a point charge, and E = V/d for a uniform field between parallel plates. It includes the inverse square law behaviour of point charge fields and the calculation of electric force using F = qE.
subtopic.why: These formulas are the quantitative foundation of the entire topic. They appear in almost every VCAA exam question on electric fields, and being able to select and apply the correct formula — point charge versus uniform field — is a critical distinguishing skill at this level.

items.title: I can calculate the electric force on a charged particle in an electric field using F = qE
items.what: The electric force on a particle with charge q in an electric field of strength E is F = qE. The direction of the force is in the direction of the field for a positive charge, and opposite to the field for a negative charge.
items.why: This formula connects the field concept to the measurable force experienced by a particle. It is the electric equivalent of F = mg for gravity, and it is used in every question involving the motion or equilibrium of a charged particle in an electric field.
items.example: An electron (charge = −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) is placed in a uniform electric field of 1000 N C⁻¹ directed downward. The force on the electron is F = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1000 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ N, directed upward (opposite to the field because the charge is negative).

subtopic.name: Electric Field Calculations
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the two key formulas for electric field strength: E = kQ/r² for a point charge, and E = V/d for a uniform field between parallel plates. It includes the inverse square law behaviour of point charge fields and the calculation of electric force using F = qE.
subtopic.why: These formulas are the quantitative foundation of the entire topic. They appear in almost every VCAA exam question on electric fields, and being able to select and apply the correct formula — point charge versus uniform field — is a critical distinguishing skill at this level.

items.title: I can compare the electric field formula and the gravitational field formula and identify similarities and differences
items.what: Both E = kQ/r² and g = GM/r² follow the inverse square law. Both fields give force per unit of the relevant quantity (force per coulomb for E; force per kilogram for g). The key difference is that electric charges can be positive or negative, so electric fields can repel as well as attract, while gravitational fields only attract.
items.why: Comparing the two field types is explicitly required in the study design. Being able to articulate both the mathematical parallels and the key physical difference (repulsion versus attraction only) is an important conceptual skill for extended response questions.
items.example: For a gravitational field: g = GM/r² and F = mg, with g in N kg⁻¹. For an electric field: E = kQ/r² and F = qE, with E in N C⁻¹. Both follow inverse square laws, and both define field strength as force per unit quantity. However, a mass always attracts while a charge can attract or repel depending on the sign of the charges involved.

subtopic.name: Electric Field Calculations
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the two key formulas for electric field strength: E = kQ/r² for a point charge, and E = V/d for a uniform field between parallel plates. It includes the inverse square law behaviour of point charge fields and the calculation of electric force using F = qE.
subtopic.why: These formulas are the quantitative foundation of the entire topic. They appear in almost every VCAA exam question on electric fields, and being able to select and apply the correct formula — point charge versus uniform field — is a critical distinguishing skill at this level.

items.title: I can state Coulomb's law and identify what each symbol represents
items.what: Coulomb's law states that the force between two point charges q₁ and q₂ separated by distance r is F = kq₁q₂/r², where k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². The force is repulsive if the charges are the same sign and attractive if they are opposite signs. The distance r is measured between the centres of the charges.
items.why: Coulomb's law is directly analogous to Newton's law of universal gravitation, F = Gm₁m₂/r². Understanding this parallel helps consolidate both topics. The law applies only when the charged objects are small relative to the distance between them (point charges).
items.example: Two metal spheres, one with charge +1.0 × 10⁻⁸ C and another with charge +1.0 × 10⁻⁹ C, are 30 cm (0.30 m) apart. The force between them is F = (9.0 × 10⁹ × 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ × 1.0 × 10⁻⁹) / (0.30)² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ N, repulsive.

subtopic.name: Coulomb's Law and Electric Force
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Coulomb's law for the force between two point charges, the inverse square dependence of electric force on distance, Newton's third law applied to electric forces between pairs of charges, and how to find the location where the net electric field or force is zero between two charges.
subtopic.why: Coulomb's law is the direct electrostatic analogue of Newton's law of universal gravitation, and mastering it consolidates understanding of both topics. Questions involving forces between charges, Newton's third law pairs, and zero-field points appear regularly in VCAA exams.

items.title: I can apply the inverse square law to predict how the electric force changes when distance is changed
items.what: Because F ∝ 1/r², doubling the distance between two charges reduces the force to one-quarter of its original value. Tripling the distance reduces the force to one-ninth. Halving the distance increases the force to four times its original value.
items.why: This ratio reasoning is tested directly in VCAA multiple-choice questions and in extended response justification questions. It allows rapid prediction of force changes without full recalculation.
items.example: Two positive charges exert a force F on each other at distance r. When the distance is doubled to 2r, the new force is F/4. When the distance is tripled to 3r, the new force is F/9. This can be verified: if F = kq₁q₂/r², then at 2r, F_new = kq₁q₂/(2r)² = kq₁q₂/4r² = F/4.

subtopic.name: Coulomb's Law and Electric Force
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Coulomb's law for the force between two point charges, the inverse square dependence of electric force on distance, Newton's third law applied to electric forces between pairs of charges, and how to find the location where the net electric field or force is zero between two charges.
subtopic.why: Coulomb's law is the direct electrostatic analogue of Newton's law of universal gravitation, and mastering it consolidates understanding of both topics. Questions involving forces between charges, Newton's third law pairs, and zero-field points appear regularly in VCAA exams.

items.title: I can apply Newton's third law to the electric forces between two charges
items.what: The force that charge A exerts on charge B is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force that charge B exerts on charge A, regardless of the relative sizes of the charges. Both forces act along the line joining the centres of the two charges.
items.why: A common misconception is that the larger charge exerts a greater force. Newton's third law means the forces are always equal in magnitude, and examiners target this misconception in MCQ distractors. This result also means changing the charge on one object affects both forces equally.
items.example: A charge of +4Q and a charge of +Q are placed at distance r apart. The force on +Q due to +4Q has the same magnitude as the force on +4Q due to +Q. Both forces are repulsive and equal F = k(4Q)(Q)/r². The smaller charge does not experience a larger force, despite the size difference.

subtopic.name: Coulomb's Law and Electric Force
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Coulomb's law for the force between two point charges, the inverse square dependence of electric force on distance, Newton's third law applied to electric forces between pairs of charges, and how to find the location where the net electric field or force is zero between two charges.
subtopic.why: Coulomb's law is the direct electrostatic analogue of Newton's law of universal gravitation, and mastering it consolidates understanding of both topics. Questions involving forces between charges, Newton's third law pairs, and zero-field points appear regularly in VCAA exams.

items.title: I can predict how the force between two charges changes when one or both charges are changed
items.what: Because F ∝ q₁q₂, the electric force is directly proportional to the product of the charges. Doubling one charge doubles the force on both objects. Doubling both charges quadruples the force. This proportionality applies at constant separation.
items.why: VCAA exam questions regularly ask students to reason about changes in force when charge magnitudes are altered, often in table-format MCQs. Being able to reason multiplicatively about the product q₁q₂ is a required skill.
items.example: Two charges +q produce a repulsive force F. If the left charge is changed to +2q and the right charge remains +q, the new force is F_new = k(2q)(q)/r² = 2F. If both are changed to +2q, the new force is k(2q)(2q)/r² = 4F.

subtopic.name: Coulomb's Law and Electric Force
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Coulomb's law for the force between two point charges, the inverse square dependence of electric force on distance, Newton's third law applied to electric forces between pairs of charges, and how to find the location where the net electric field or force is zero between two charges.
subtopic.why: Coulomb's law is the direct electrostatic analogue of Newton's law of universal gravitation, and mastering it consolidates understanding of both topics. Questions involving forces between charges, Newton's third law pairs, and zero-field points appear regularly in VCAA exams.

items.title: I can find the position where the net electric field is zero between two point charges
items.what: Between two charges, there is a point where the electric fields from each charge cancel. For two positive charges, this point lies on the line between them, closer to the smaller charge. The position is found by setting the two field expressions equal: kQ₁/r₁² = kQ₂/r₂², where r₁ + r₂ equals the total separation.
items.why: This multi-step problem type requires students to set up and solve simultaneous equations, combining the inverse square law with spatial reasoning. It appears as an extended response question and tests whether students understand field direction as well as magnitude.
items.example: Two positive charges Q₁ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ C and Q₂ = 8.0 × 10⁻⁸ C are 30 cm apart. The zero-field point is at distance r₁ from Q₁, where kQ₁/r₁² = kQ₂/(0.30 − r₁)². Solving gives r₁ = 10 cm from Q₁. The zero-field point is closer to the smaller charge Q₁.

subtopic.name: Coulomb's Law and Electric Force
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Coulomb's law for the force between two point charges, the inverse square dependence of electric force on distance, Newton's third law applied to electric forces between pairs of charges, and how to find the location where the net electric field or force is zero between two charges.
subtopic.why: Coulomb's law is the direct electrostatic analogue of Newton's law of universal gravitation, and mastering it consolidates understanding of both topics. Questions involving forces between charges, Newton's third law pairs, and zero-field points appear regularly in VCAA exams.

items.title: I can calculate the work done on a charged particle moving through a potential difference using W = qV
items.what: The work done on a charged particle with charge q moving through a potential difference V is W = qV, measured in joules. This work equals the change in kinetic energy of the particle if no other forces act on it. The potential difference V is the voltage between the start and end points.
items.why: W = qV is one of the most frequently applied formulas in the entire electric fields topic. It connects the macroscopic voltage (which can be measured on a voltmeter) to the energy gained by a microscopic charged particle, and it is used in all electron gun and particle accelerator calculations.
items.example: An electron (charge = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 5000 V. The work done on the electron is W = qV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5000 = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁶ J. This work is converted entirely to kinetic energy, so Ek = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁶ J.

subtopic.name: Electric Potential Energy and Work
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers work done on a charged particle moving through a potential difference using W = qV, qualitative understanding of electric potential energy changes in both uniform and non-uniform electric fields, and how the area under a force–distance graph gives the change in electric potential energy.
subtopic.why: Electric potential energy and work are the energy aspects of electric fields, mirroring gravitational potential energy in Chapter 3. The formula W = qV is used in every question involving particle accelerators, electron guns, and charges moving between plates.

items.title: I can qualitatively describe how electric potential energy changes as a positive or negative charge moves in a uniform electric field
items.what: In a uniform electric field, a positive charge gains kinetic energy and loses electric potential energy when it moves in the direction of the field (from the positive plate toward the negative plate). Moving against the field increases its electric potential energy. For a negative charge, the directions of energy change are reversed.
items.why: Qualitative reasoning about potential energy direction — without calculation — is explicitly required in the study design and tested in exam questions asking whether potential energy increases or decreases. The parallel with gravitational potential energy (mass falling loses Eg) helps with reasoning.
items.example: A proton placed at the positive plate of a parallel plate capacitor and released will accelerate toward the negative plate. As it moves, it loses electric potential energy and gains kinetic energy. A released electron at the same plate would move in the opposite direction — toward the positive plate — and also lose electric potential energy and gain kinetic energy.

subtopic.name: Electric Potential Energy and Work
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers work done on a charged particle moving through a potential difference using W = qV, qualitative understanding of electric potential energy changes in both uniform and non-uniform electric fields, and how the area under a force–distance graph gives the change in electric potential energy.
subtopic.why: Electric potential energy and work are the energy aspects of electric fields, mirroring gravitational potential energy in Chapter 3. The formula W = qV is used in every question involving particle accelerators, electron guns, and charges moving between plates.

items.title: I can qualitatively describe how electric potential energy changes as a charge moves in a non-uniform electric field around a point charge
items.what: When a positive charge is pushed closer to another positive charge (against the repulsive force), work is done against the field and electric potential energy increases. When released, the stored potential energy converts to kinetic energy as the charge moves away. Moving a positive charge toward a negative charge reduces electric potential energy.
items.why: The qualitative treatment of non-uniform fields is required by the study design. It is also the conceptual basis for understanding particle accelerators and for interpreting force–distance graphs, and it extends naturally from the gravitational potential energy concept in Chapter 3.
items.example: A positive charge +q is pushed from point B (far from a central +Q) to point A (closer to +Q). Work is done against the repulsive force. The electric potential energy at A is greater than at B by an amount equal to the area under the force–distance graph between B and A. If released at A, the charge accelerates outward and recovers this energy as kinetic energy at point B.

subtopic.name: Electric Potential Energy and Work
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers work done on a charged particle moving through a potential difference using W = qV, qualitative understanding of electric potential energy changes in both uniform and non-uniform electric fields, and how the area under a force–distance graph gives the change in electric potential energy.
subtopic.why: Electric potential energy and work are the energy aspects of electric fields, mirroring gravitational potential energy in Chapter 3. The formula W = qV is used in every question involving particle accelerators, electron guns, and charges moving between plates.

items.title: I can determine the change in electric potential energy from the area under a force–distance graph
items.what: The area under an electric force–distance graph represents the work done on or by the electric force, which equals the change in electric potential energy. For a positive charge moving toward another positive charge, the area under the graph gives the increase in electric potential energy.
items.why: This graphical method is directly analogous to the gravitational force–distance graph method required in Chapter 3. It is tested in VCAA exam questions where a graph is provided and students must estimate the area by counting squares to find the energy change.
items.example: A force–distance graph shows the repulsive force between two positive charges, with the force decreasing from 0.1 MN near the charge to near zero at large distances. If a test charge is moved from point B to point A (closer to the central charge), the shaded area under the curve between those two points gives the change in electric potential energy in joules.

subtopic.name: Electric Potential Energy and Work
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers work done on a charged particle moving through a potential difference using W = qV, qualitative understanding of electric potential energy changes in both uniform and non-uniform electric fields, and how the area under a force–distance graph gives the change in electric potential energy.
subtopic.why: Electric potential energy and work are the energy aspects of electric fields, mirroring gravitational potential energy in Chapter 3. The formula W = qV is used in every question involving particle accelerators, electron guns, and charges moving between plates.

items.title: I can use W = qV to find the kinetic energy and speed of a particle accelerated from rest between parallel plates
items.what: When a charged particle is accelerated from rest through a potential difference V, all of the work done W = qV is converted to kinetic energy: qV = ½mv². Rearranging gives the exit speed as v = √(2qV/m). This calculation assumes the particle starts from rest and no energy is lost to other forces.
items.why: This multi-step calculation — linking voltage to kinetic energy to speed — is one of the most common extended response question types in the electric fields section of VCAA exams. It is the basis for understanding electron guns and particle accelerators.
items.example: A proton (mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) is accelerated from rest through 100 V. Work done: W = qV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 100 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ J. Setting equal to ½mv²: v = √(2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ / 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷) = 1.38 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

subtopic.name: Electric Potential Energy and Work
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers work done on a charged particle moving through a potential difference using W = qV, qualitative understanding of electric potential energy changes in both uniform and non-uniform electric fields, and how the area under a force–distance graph gives the change in electric potential energy.
subtopic.why: Electric potential energy and work are the energy aspects of electric fields, mirroring gravitational potential energy in Chapter 3. The formula W = qV is used in every question involving particle accelerators, electron guns, and charges moving between plates.

items.title: I can calculate the magnitude of the electric force on a charged particle between parallel plates using F = qE
items.what: The electric force on a charged particle of charge q in a uniform field of strength E is F = qE. In the uniform region between parallel plates, this force is constant in magnitude and direction. For a positive charge, the force is in the direction of the field (toward the negative plate); for a negative charge, the force is opposite to the field.
items.why: F = qE is the starting point for all motion calculations involving charged particles between plates. It determines both the direction of deflection (which identifies the sign of the charge) and the magnitude of the acceleration (via F = ma), which determines the deflection distance.
items.example: An electron (charge = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) is between plates with E = 1000 N C⁻¹. The force on the electron is F = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1000 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ N. Because the electron is negatively charged, the force is directed opposite to the field — toward the positive plate.

subtopic.name: Charged Particles in Uniform Fields
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the behaviour of charged particles entering and moving through uniform electric fields, including the constant force F = qE acting perpendicular to the initial velocity, the resulting parabolic path, and how changes to charge, mass, speed, or field strength affect the deflection of a particle.
subtopic.why: Charged particle motion in uniform fields is the electric analogue of projectile motion in a gravitational field. It underpins the operation of electron guns, cathode ray tubes, and particle accelerators, and it is regularly tested in extended response questions asking students to justify changes in deflection.

items.title: I can describe and explain the parabolic path of a charged particle entering a uniform electric field perpendicular to its initial velocity
items.what: When a charged particle enters a uniform electric field at right angles to the field direction, it experiences a constant force perpendicular to its initial velocity. Its horizontal velocity component remains unchanged while it accelerates vertically, producing a parabolic path. This is directly analogous to projectile motion in a gravitational field.
items.why: The parabolic path result is required conceptual knowledge. Understanding why it is parabolic (constant force perpendicular to constant horizontal velocity) allows students to justify their answers in questions that ask whether the path is parabolic, circular, or linear.
items.example: A positive particle enters horizontally between two vertical charged plates. The electric field points downward (toward the negative plate). The particle continues at constant horizontal speed while accelerating downward, tracing a parabola. This is the same shape as a horizontally launched projectile in Earth's gravitational field.

subtopic.name: Charged Particles in Uniform Fields
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the behaviour of charged particles entering and moving through uniform electric fields, including the constant force F = qE acting perpendicular to the initial velocity, the resulting parabolic path, and how changes to charge, mass, speed, or field strength affect the deflection of a particle.
subtopic.why: Charged particle motion in uniform fields is the electric analogue of projectile motion in a gravitational field. It underpins the operation of electron guns, cathode ray tubes, and particle accelerators, and it is regularly tested in extended response questions asking students to justify changes in deflection.

items.title: I can determine the sign of a charge from the direction of its deflection in a uniform electric field
items.what: A positive charge deflects in the direction of the electric field (toward the negative plate). A negative charge deflects opposite to the electric field direction (toward the positive plate). The direction of deflection is the key evidence for determining the sign of a charge in an experiment.
items.why: Identifying charge sign from deflection direction is a standard VCAA exam question type, appearing in both MCQ and extended response. It requires students to reason from the field direction convention (defined by the force on a positive test charge) to the actual force on the particle in question.
items.example: A charged particle enters a horizontal uniform electric field directed upward (from negative plate at bottom to positive plate at top). The particle deflects downward. Since the force is opposite to the field, the particle must be negatively charged. A positive particle would have deflected upward, in the direction of the field.

items.title: I can justify whether the force on a charged particle in a uniform electric field is constant or changing
items.what: In a uniform electric field, the electric field strength E is constant at all points. Therefore, the force F = qE on a charged particle is also constant in magnitude and direction throughout the field — as long as the particle remains between the plates. Once the particle exits the field, the force drops to zero.
items.why: Students often incorrectly state that the force changes as a particle moves through the field (confusing uniform fields with non-uniform point charge fields). Explaining that F is constant because E is constant in a uniform field is an important distinction that is directly tested.
items.example: A proton enters from the left between two horizontal charged plates with the field directed downward. At every position between the plates — whether the proton is near the entry point or near the exit — the force on it is the same: F = qE, directed downward. The force only ceases when the proton exits from between the plates.

items.title: I can predict and justify changes to the deflection of a charged particle when its speed, charge, or the field strength is changed
items.what: Increasing the particle's entry speed reduces the deflection (less time between the plates for the same transverse acceleration). Increasing the field strength E increases the deflection (greater transverse force). Increasing the charge q also increases deflection. Increasing the mass m reduces deflection (less acceleration for the same force).
items.why: These qualitative predictions — with justification — are a standard extended response question type at VCAA. Each change must be traced through a causal chain: change in variable → change in force or time → change in deflection.
items.example: A particle enters the field at speed v and is deflected a distance d. If the entry speed is doubled to 2v, the particle spends half the time in the field, so the transverse displacement is reduced (d decreases). If a new particle with the same charge but half the mass enters at the same speed, the acceleration doubles, so the deflection increases.

items.title: I can explain how a uniform electric field is used to accelerate a charged particle in a particle accelerator
items.what: In the electron gun section of a particle accelerator, a uniform electric field between two parallel plates accelerates charged particles from rest. The work done by the field (W = qV) is converted to kinetic energy. Linear acceleration uses electric fields, while changes in direction are produced by magnetic fields.
items.why: Particle accelerators are a key application explicitly listed in the study design. Understanding the role of the uniform electric field in linear acceleration, as distinct from the role of magnetic fields in path-bending, is required conceptual knowledge for the synchrotron topic.
items.example: In the electron gun of a particle accelerator, electrons start from rest near the negative plate and are accelerated through a potential difference of 5000 V toward the positive plate. By the time they exit, they have gained kinetic energy of qV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5000 = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁶ J, reaching a speed of approximately 4.2 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.
